extracted.intended_audience: readers of satire, students/practitioners of humor and rhetoric, and general educated readers interested in Renaissance humanist critique
extracted.subtask_short: satirical essay: folly and humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpt from a Renaissance satirical essay (Erasmus' Praise of Folly) arguing that folly underpins social life, entertainment, politics, and the arts; contains many implicit principles about what makes social amusement, comedy, and persuasive spectacle effective. Useful as a source of precepts for comedic writing, satire, and social humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folly as necessary social lubricant
rubrics_metrics.description: The more folly various amusements have, the more they conduce to human life; without such diversions life would be unpleasant and not deserve the name of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: feasts, jests, merriments, dancing, games. 'The nature of all which things is such that the more of folly they have, the more they conduce to human life.' Use folly to wipe away tediousness and make social life tolerable and delightful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hire buffoons/entertainers when laughter is lacking
rubrics_metrics.description: When a company lacks occasion for laughter they 'send for one that may make it,' or hire a buffoon/flatterer whose ridiculous discourse dispels gravity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical anti‑pattern: leaving feasts without comic relief. Positive examples: hiring entertainers, choosing a king for the table, throwing dice, drinking healths, trolling it round, dancing the cushion. Use intentional comic performers or staged games to generate merriment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve theatrical disguise; don't strip performers of their role
rubrics_metrics.description: Revealing an actor's disguise ruins the design of the play and the pleasure of the spectators; comedy depends on characters sustaining their parts and masks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not 'strip' the player's disguise in public critique; exposing the artifice spoils entertainment and may provoke anger. Maintain the illusion — role‑playing and disguise are central devices of comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flattery and myth as effective political persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Fables, symbolic inventions, and flattery — not philosophical orations — have moved and disciplined the common people and built cities and empires.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples offered: Amphion and Orpheus' harp, Themistocles' tales, Sertorius' white hind, Minos and Numa ruling by fabulous inventions. Use simple fable, striking emblem, or flattering myth to persuade popular audiences rather than abstruse reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlooking friends' faults (euetheian) sustains friendship
rubrics_metrics.description: To wink at, be blind to, or admire friends' vices (even as virtues) is a form of folly that joins and continues friendships; mutual tolerance of imperfections is social glue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: kissing a mistress' freckle or a father praising a squint-eyed child. Anti‑pattern: being eagle‑sighted about friends' faults and blear‑eyed about one's own — this destroys friendship. For social harmony favor lenience and fond exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folly preserves marriages via flattery and connivance
rubrics_metrics.description: Most marriages endure because husbands and wives flatter one another, dissemble, and prudently connive at each other's faults; a too‑thorough examination of a spouse's past would dissolve many unions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: husbands neglecting wives' prior tricks, women using beauty and foolishness to please. Anti‑pattern: excessive scrutiny and exposing every past action. For domestic harmony, promote pleasant self‑deception and small deceptions of affection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-love and self‑flattery as precondition for public praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Everyone must flatter and commend themselves to themselves before they can be commended by others; being able to applaud oneself makes external censure less harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you can 'applaud yourself' then public hissing matters little. Cultivate self‑regard (within the essay's comic frame) to sustain confidence in social performance; anti‑pattern: total self‑abnegation that seeks only external validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Folly (bold ignorance) enables practical action and experiential prudence
rubrics_metrics.description: Fools, free from modesty and fear, attempt and venture into the world and thereby acquire true prudence through experience, whereas the wise man, through modesty and distrust, often attempts nothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation: 'The fool ... gathers, if I mistake not, the true prudence, such as Homer though blind may be said to have seen when he said, "The burnt child dreads the fire."' Encourages learning by doing; anti‑pattern: paralysis by overcaution and book‑bound subtleties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Favor natural simplicity and 'folly‑adjacent' arts over abstruse sciences
rubrics_metrics.description: Arts that come nearest to common sense (and thus to folly) are most esteemed by the public; pure abstruse learning often alienates people and is less conducive to happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: physicians and lawyers (practical arts) are more rewarded than divines or logicians. 'Nature hates all false coloring' — prefer unadulterated, practical expression over artifice and excessive technicality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fable, emblem, and ridiculous symbol to move crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Popular actions and great heroic deeds are often rooted in empty vainglory and symbolic tales rather than dry philosophy; simple, striking tales mobilize people more effectively than rational argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the Decii, Q. Curtius, Sertorius' inventions. For mass persuasion, deploy memorable images and stories; anti‑pattern: relying on philosophical exhortation to rally the populace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't be unseasonably wise — fit your wisdom to the occasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Unseasonable or forward prudence (speaking truths that contradict common opinion at the wrong time) is foolish; it is better to 'order oneself as the market goes' — either ignore the world or run with it for company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti‑pattern: publicly disproving commonly received opinions at a feast or social gathering. Practical rule: adapt your tone and content to social context; theatrical civility and timing matter more than relentless truth‑telling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passions (the components of folly) are incentives to virtuous action
rubrics_metrics.description: Passions — though attributed to Folly — serve as spurs, incentives, and tutors to virtue and action; removing all affection (as some Stoics desire) would leave a man inhuman and ineffectual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of Stoic ideal: eliminating affections makes a man 'a new kind of god' and useless for social life. Use emotional energy (love, pity, ambition) to motivate characters and actions rather than suppressing feeling for abstract correctness.
